The triple pun on 'light' (luminous / wanton / trivial) is textually grounded — Jessica's own next line ('office of discovery… I should be obscur'd') confirms she means the torch reveals her shameful disguise — and 'too-too' as an intensifier is well established; the annotation correctly avoids over-sexualising the pun.

anchor_text: gild myself With some moe ducats
summary: Jessica says she will 'gild' herself with more ducats before coming down — meaning she will load herself with more of her father's gold coins. 'Gild' means to coat with gold, but since she is literally taking gold (the ducats), the word doubles as a pun: she is both beautifying herself and covering herself in Shylock's gold. 'Moe' is an archaic form of 'more.'
detail: The pun is darkly pointed. To gild is to overlay something base with gold — the same logic that misleads Morocco at the gold casket ('All that glisters is not gold,' 2.7). Jessica's casual 'gilding' of herself with stolen money performs the elopement's moral ambiguity: she is a daughter robbing her father, and the language of ornament and gold-coating quietly touches the play's running question about what shines and what is worth. 'Ducats' were the standard Venetian gold coin; Shylock's anguished later cry 'My ducats and my daughter' (2.8, reported by Salarino) makes Jessica's parting grab here the more resonant.

anchor_text: a Gentile, and no Jew
summary: Gratiano's remark that Jessica is 'a Gentile, and no Jew' uses 'Gentile' with a pun: in its religious sense it means non-Jewish (a Christian), but it also sounds like 'gentle' (well-born, gracious, of gentle blood). Gratiano means that Jessica has a Christian soul despite her Jewish birth — a distinction the play treats as both a compliment and, from a modern perspective, a deeply troubling one.
detail: The pun on Gentile/gentle was audible to Elizabethan ears and is exploited elsewhere in the play (Launcelot in 3.5 makes it explicit: 'Yes truly; for, look you, the sins of the father are to be laid upon the children... the Jew's daughter... I shall answer that better to the commonwealth than you can the getting up of the Negro's belly'). Gratiano's casual relief that Jessica is 'no Jew' reflects the period's fusion of ethnic and religious identity in the figure of 'the Jew.' For the play's antisemitic framing and Elizabethan stage conventions, see the reference card below.

anchor_text: Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire
summary: Each casket carries a set motto that functions as a riddle: gold promises what 'many men desire' (Portia herself, or worldly wealth), silver promises 'as much as he deserves' (pride in one's own merit), and lead demands a suitor 'give and hazard all he hath' (selfless risk). The correct choice is lead. The test originates in the Gesta Romanorum, a medieval collection of moralised tales, where the caskets carry inverted mottoes to expose greed and vanity.
detail: Shakespeare's source is the Gesta Romanorum ('Deeds of the Romans'), a Latin compilation of tales assembled around 1300 and translated into English by Richard Robinson in 1577. There the caskets hold bones, earth, and jewels respectively; Shakespeare reverses the prizes so that lead — the humblest outward appearance — contains the greatest reward. The three mottoes frame the play's central warning that 'All that glisters is not gold': Morocco reasons toward gold by desire and superficial glory; Arragon toward silver by self-assessed worth; Bassanio away from both by distrusting ornament.

anchor_text: The Hyrcanian deserts and the vasty wilds
summary: Hyrcania was the ancient name for the wild, forested region south and east of the Caspian Sea (roughly modern Iran and Turkmenistan). Classical writers used it as a byword for the edge of the known world and extreme savagery; tigers from there ('Hyrcanian tiger') recur in Shakespeare as emblems of ferocity. Morocco uses the name to picture suitors crossing the whole known world — from the farthest east to 'wide Arabia' — just to see Portia.

anchor_text: The watery kingdom, whose ambitious head / Spits in the face of heaven
summary: Morocco personifies the sea as a proud kingdom whose waves ('ambitious head') reach up and 'spit in the face of heaven' — yet even the ocean is no barrier to princes racing to Belmont. 'Ambitious' here means literally 'striving upward' (from Latin ambitio, a going around, but often connoting overreach). The image of waves thrusting toward the sky was a Renaissance commonplace for the sea's dangerous pride, and Morocco turns it into a measure of the world's desire for Portia.

The personification and the sense of 'ambitious' as 'striving upward' are sound, but deriving 'ambitious' from 'ambitio meaning a going around' and then glossing it as connoting overreach is a folk-etymology digression — ambitio primarily means 'canvassing' or 'going around to seek votes'; the sense here is simply 'high-aspiring,' and the etymology note muddies rather than clarifies the gloss.

anchor_text: To rib her cerecloth in the obscure grave
summary: A 'cerecloth' (also 'cerement') is a winding-sheet saturated in wax used to wrap a corpse for burial. To 'rib' it means to encase or enclose within it, as ribs enclose the chest. Morocco is saying it would be a sin to imagine Portia's picture shut inside a wax-wrapped corpse's shroud in a dark grave — the lead casket's dull heaviness reads to him as burial.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cerecloth': 'cloth smeared with wax or other glutinous matter, used to wrap a corpse.' Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'cerecloth.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 954
OED s.v. 'cerecloth' and Onions' Shakespeare Glossary are real authorities and the definition given matches their entries accurately.

The definitions of 'cerecloth' as a wax-impregnated winding-sheet and 'rib' as 'encase' are standard and lexicographically supported; the reading of Morocco's logic — lead reads to him as burial — is exactly what the text says.

anchor_text: in silver she's immur'd, / Being ten times undervalu'd to tried gold
summary: 'Immured' means walled in or imprisoned (from Latin murus, wall). Morocco dismisses the silver casket because silver is 'ten times undervalu'd to tried gold' — silver was worth roughly one-tenth the price of gold by weight in standard Elizabethan exchange rates. 'Tried' means tested or refined (gold that has been proved pure by assay). His logic is sound but leads him to the wrong answer: the test is about humility, not market value.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'immure': 'to enclose within walls; to confine, imprison.' Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'tried': 'proved genuine by the test of fire.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 955
OED s.v. 'immure' and Schmidt s.v. 'tried' are standard reference works and the definitions cited are accurate.

The vocabulary glosses ('immured,' 'tried') are correct, but the claim that silver was 'worth roughly one-tenth the price of gold by weight in standard Elizabethan exchange rates' is presented as a precise fact when the gold-to-silver ratio in Elizabethan England fluctuated significantly and was typically closer to 1:12 to 1:14 by weight; Morocco's 'ten times' is rhetoric, not a market rate, and the gloss risks literalizing the figure.

anchor_text: A coin that bears the figure of an angel / Stamped in gold; but that's insculp'd upon; / But here an angel in a golden bed
summary: The 'angel' was a real English gold coin stamped with the image of the Archangel Michael slaying a dragon; it was in circulation from the 1460s until the 1640s and worth ten shillings. Morocco puns on it: the English coin has a mere image of an angel pressed ('insculp'd') onto its surface, but the gold casket contains — he reasons — an actual angelic being (Portia) resting inside 'a golden bed.' The pun flatters Portia as worth infinitely more than a coin.
detail: The gold angel coin was one of the most recognizable English coins of the period, issued first under Edward IV (1465) and still struck under James I; it showed St Michael on the obverse with a ship on the reverse. 'Insculp'd' means 'engraved upon' (Latin insculpo). Morocco's distinction — mere image on the outside versus the real thing inside — ironically inverts the play's whole lesson: he is choosing the casket whose worth is all surface, its golden show enclosing a death's-head rather than a portrait.

sources.name: OED; Challis, A New History of the Royal Mint
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'angel,' sense 4: 'A gold coin bearing the device of the archangel Michael'; C. E. Challis, A New History of the Royal Mint (1992), pp. 200-202 (the English angel coin, value 10 shillings, 1465-1642).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 959

The OED angel sense 4 and Challis's A New History of the Royal Mint are real; the angel coin was worth 10 shillings during Elizabeth I's reign (from 1562 onward) and was last minted under Charles I in 1642.

The identification of the 'angel' as the English gold coin stamped with St Michael, its value at ten shillings, and the wordplay on image-versus-reality are all accurate and the ironic inversion — Morocco chooses the surface-value coin just as he chooses the casket by surface — is a mainstream, well-supported interpretive point.

anchor_text: All that glisters is not gold, / Often have you heard that told
summary: 'Glisters' is an older form of 'glistens' or 'glitters' (Elizabethan English used both forms interchangeably). The scroll mocks Morocco for doing exactly what the proverb warns against: choosing by surface shine rather than inner worth. The casket is the test made visible -- its glittering gold exterior hides a death's-head and a poem ending 'your suit is cold.' The saying was already proverbial before Shakespeare, who gives it its most memorable form here.
detail: The proverb is found in English long before the play: a variant appears in Chaucer's Canon's Yeoman's Tale, and the idea recurs in medieval Latin (Alanus de Insulis). The rhymed scroll (gold / told / sold / behold / infold / bold / old / inscroll'd / cold) is in strict tetrameter couplets -- a formally contemptuous jingle, as if the punishment itself is a nursery-rhyme. 'Gilded tombs do worms infold' picks up the resonance from Morocco's own earlier fear of 'ribbing' Portia 'in the obscure grave': the grave he imagined for the lead casket is exactly what the gold casket represents.

sources.name: Tilley, A Dictionary of the Proverbs in England
sources.citation: M. P. Tilley, A Dictionary of the Proverbs in England in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries (1950), A146: 'All is not gold that glitters' (with antecedents in Chaucer's Canon's Yeoman's Tale and earlier). OED s.v. 'glister.'

anchor_text: A gentle riddance. Draw the curtains: go. / Let all of his complexion choose me so.
summary: 'Complexion' means skin colour (also bodily constitution and humour, but the primary meaning here is racial). Portia's relief — 'a gentle riddance' means a good getting-rid-of — ends with a line expressing prejudice against Morocco's Moorish race: she hopes every man of his colouring makes the same wrong choice. Morocco himself had asked her not to judge him 'for my complexion' (2.1). The line frames the casket plot within the play's broader, troubled treatment of race.
detail: Morocco's two scenes (2.1 and 2.7) sit at the intersection of two prejudices the play uses and dramatizes: the stage-Moor as exotic outsider (see the-moor-on-the-english-stage) and the casket test as an exposure of worldly pride. Portia's aside is unambiguous in its hostility and has caused discomfort in performance from at least the eighteenth century. It sits uncomfortably against the play's own scene structure, which devotes more space to Morocco's courtship than to Arragon's and gives him the most rhetorical dignity of the two failed suitors. 'Gentle riddance' uses 'gentle' in the sense of 'good' or 'welcome.'

sources.name: OED; Cowhig, 'Actors Black and Tawny in the Role of Othello'
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'complexion,' sense 1a: 'physical constitution as determined by the proportion of the four humours; also external appearance, skin colour.' Ruth Cowhig, 'Actors Black and Tawny in the Role of Othello and Their Audience,' Theatre Research International 4 (1979), on stage Moors and racial coding in the Elizabethan theatre.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 982

OED s.v. 'complexion' is correctly cited; the Cowhig article is real (Theatre Research International 4, 1979) but its scope is specifically the stage history of Othello rather than Elizabethan racial coding broadly, so it only partially supports the wider claim made.

The reading of 'complexion' as skin colour (with secondary humour-sense acknowledged) is correct, and characterising Portia's closing couplet as an expression of racial prejudice is mainstream scholarly consensus rather than an anachronistic over-reading; noting the tension between this aside and Morocco's rhetorical dignity in the scene is a responsible, balanced gloss.

anchor_text: The villain Jew with outcries rais'd the Duke
summary: Salanio calls Shylock 'the villain Jew,' treating his religion as a sufficient label for villainy. The phrase reflects the Elizabethan stage convention of the predatory Jewish moneylender — a figure drawn from imagination rather than experience, since Jews had been expelled from England in 1290 and were not formally readmitted until 1656.
detail: The stock figure reaches Shakespeare via Marlowe's Barabas in The Jew of Malta (c. 1590), played at the same Rose Theatre where Shakespeare's company performed. The trial of Elizabeth I's Portuguese-Jewish physician Rodrigo Lopez in 1594 on a (probably fabricated) charge of plotting to poison the Queen inflamed popular prejudice in the year The Merchant of Venice was written. Salanio and Salarino speak the audience's expected contempt, but the play simultaneously gives Shylock his own voice, his own grief, and the great '3.1 protest' ('Hath not a Jew eyes?') that exceeds anything the stock type could say. The note is historical: the play presents the prejudice as a dramatic problem, not an endorsement.

sources.name: Shapiro, Shakespeare and the Jews
sources.citation: James Shapiro, Shakespeare and the Jews (Columbia UP, 1996), ch. 3-4, on the Lopez affair and the theatrical Jew.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 987

Shapiro (Columbia UP, 1996) is a real book covering the Lopez affair and the theatrical Jew figure; ch. 3 ('The Jewish Crime') and ch. 4 ('The Pound of Flesh') address both topics, though the annotator's chapter descriptions are loosely paraphrased rather than exact titles; the 1290 expulsion and 1656 readmission dates are confirmed, and the Rose Theatre connection to Marlowe's Jew of Malta is documented in Henslowe's diary.

The cultural-context gloss accurately identifies Salanio's phrase as reflecting the Elizabethan stage convention of the predatory Jewish moneylender, correctly ties it to Marlowe's Barabas and the Lopez affair, and rightly notes the play simultaneously gives Shylock his own voice — all mainstream scholarship, no overreach.

anchor_text: My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter!
summary: Salanio mimics Shylock in the street, alternating between grief for his daughter Jessica and grief for his stolen money as though the two are interchangeable. The speech is a cruel parody, not a direct quotation from Shylock — it is reported by an enemy who wants to make Shylock ridiculous. Whether Shylock actually spoke these exact words is left uncertain; what is certain is that Salanio intends the conflation of daughter and ducats to mock him.
detail: The equating of a child with money is the scene's sharpest moment of antisemitic caricature: it implies Shylock loves his gold as much as, or more than, his daughter. Yet the same speech hints at a real anguish that the parody cannot fully suppress — a father has lost a child, and he has no one in Venice to mourn with him. Later (3.1) Tubal confirms Shylock's grief over his daughter is genuine; the conflation here is the bystanders' invention, not necessarily his. Ducats were the gold coins of Venice, the principal currency of Mediterranean trade.

sources.name: Leggatt, Shakespeare's Comedies of Love
sources.citation: Alexander Leggatt, Shakespeare's Comedies of Love (Methuen, 1974), pp. 149-152, on the reported speech and its unreliability.

sources.name: OED s.v. ducat
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'ducat, n.': a gold coin used across late-medieval and Renaissance Europe, originally from the Duchy of Apulia, widely minted in Venice.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 998

The actual title of Leggatt's 1974 Methuen book is 'Shakespeare's Comedy of Love' (singular), not 'Shakespeare's Comedies of Love' (plural) as cited; the book does include a Merchant of Venice chapter, so the source is real and relevant, but the title misquotation introduces a minor unreliability; the OED ducat etymology (Duchy of Apulia origin) is confirmed correct.

The annotation correctly identifies this as Salanio's hostile parody rather than a direct quotation from Shylock, appropriately flags its unreliability as reported speech, and the note that 3.1 confirms genuine paternal grief is accurate — the reading is editorially sound and avoids both sentimental and cynical overstatement.

anchor_text: two stones, two rich and precious stones
summary: 'Stones' was Elizabethan slang for testicles, and Salarino's line 'Crying, his stones, his daughter, and his ducats' (1007) exploits the double meaning for a cheap laugh at Shylock's expense. The joke implies Shylock has lost not just his jewels but his manhood and his capacity to beget more children — a particularly cruel jest given that Jessica, the daughter who robbed him, is gone.
detail: The pun is underscored by Salanio's previous line: Shylock cried 'She hath the stones upon her.' The sexual innuendo makes Jessica's flight a symbolic castration of her father as well as a financial and personal betrayal. Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'stone') lists the sexual sense as current throughout Shakespeare. The joke belongs to the hostile male banter of Salanio and Salarino and is not a slip; it signals to the audience that their sympathy is expected to lie with the Christians laughing at Shylock.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. stone
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon and Quotation Dictionary (1874-5; rev. Sarrazin 1902), s.v. 'stone' sense 3: the testicles.

sources.name: Williams, Glossary of Shakespeare's Sexual Language
sources.citation: Gordon Williams, A Glossary of Shakespeare's Sexual Language (Athlone, 1997), s.v. 'stones.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1003

Both Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874-5, rev. Sarrazin 1902) and Gordon Williams's A Glossary of Shakespeare's Sexual Language (Athlone, 1997) are confirmed real publications; 'stones' as Elizabethan slang for testicles is well-attested in Shakespeare scholarship and both sources support the claim.

The bawdy double meaning of 'stones' as testicles is firmly established in Elizabethan English, is clearly activated by the context (Salanio picks it up at TLN 1007 with 'his stones, his daughter, and his ducats'), and the symbolic-castration reading is well within mainstream early-modern bawdy scholarship (Williams, Schmidt).

anchor_text: in the narrow seas that part The French and English
summary: The 'narrow seas' is the standard Elizabethan name for the English Channel, the strait between England and France. A French merchant has told Salarino that a richly loaded ship ('richly fraught' = carrying a valuable cargo) has been wrecked there. This report is the first concrete hint that Antonio's trading ships may be in danger of failing — the precondition for Shylock's bond becoming deadly.
detail: The Channel was notorious for storms and for piracy. Shakespeare's audience would have recognized 'the narrow seas' immediately as a hazard to English merchant shipping. The conversation sets up the play's later revelations (3.1, 3.2) of Antonio's losses: Salarino and Salanio are the rumour-bearers through whom the audience tracks the fate of Antonio's argosies. 'Fraught' (= freighted, loaded with cargo) is standard mercantile vocabulary; Onions (Shakespeare Glossary) cites it as the regular past participle of 'freight.'

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. fraught
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (Oxford, 1911; rev. Eagleson 1986), s.v. 'fraught, ppl. a.': laden, freighted.

sources.name: Hakluyt, Principal Navigations (1598-1600)
sources.citation: Richard Hakluyt, The Principal Navigations, Voyages, Traffiques and Discoveries of the English Nation (1598-1600), vol. 1-2, for the hazards of the English Channel in Elizabethan merchant trade.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1012

Onions's Shakespeare Glossary is real and the 'fraught' entry is plausible; Hakluyt's Principal Navigations (1598-1600) is a confirmed real work, but its content covers global English voyages rather than specifically the hazards of the English Channel, making the citation a loose fit for the specific claim about Channel shipping dangers.

The identification of 'the narrow seas' as the English Channel is correct Elizabethan usage, the gloss on 'fraught' as laden/freighted is accurate, and the narrative framing as the first signal of Antonio's shipping peril is defensible given the scene's dramatic function — no anachronism or overreach.

anchor_text: Slubber not business for my sake, Bassanio
summary: To 'slubber' something is to do it hastily and carelessly, to skip over it or smear it through without care. Antonio is telling Bassanio not to rush his courtship of Portia just to hurry home to Venice for Antonio's sake. The word implies hurrying so fast that you do a sloppy job — like someone daubing paint without looking.
detail: The word derives from a cloth-working term: to slubber was to draw out fibres unevenly when preparing wool for spinning, leaving lumps and tangles. By extension it came to mean any careless, slovenly action. Schmidt (Shakespeare-Lexicon) and OED both record it in this figurative sense; Onions notes the single surviving metaphorical use in Shakespeare is this passage. Antonio's generosity is the dramatic point: he actively tells Bassanio to take his time winning Portia and not let the Shylock bond disturb his courtship.

sources.name: OED s.v. slubber
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'slubber, v.' sense 2: 'to perform in a careless, hurried, or slovenly manner; to do superficially or imperfectly.' First attested c. 1530.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. slubber
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon and Quotation Dictionary (1874-5; rev. Sarrazin 1902), s.v. 'slubber.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1023

OED 'slubber, v.' sense 2 ('to perform in a careless, hurried, or slovenly manner') with first attestation c. 1530 is confirmed; Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon is a real reference work; both sources accurately support the archaic vocabulary claim.

The core gloss (to do carelessly or hastily) and the cloth-working etymology are correct, but the detail section's claim that Onions notes this as 'the single surviving metaphorical use in Shakespeare' is factually wrong — 'slubber' also appears in Othello 1.3 ('slubber the gloss of your new fortunes'), undermining the note's reliability even though the word-sense itself is sound.

anchor_text: his eye being big with tears, Turning his face, he put his hand behind him
summary: Antonio turns away to hide his tears, reaches his hand back without looking, and wrings Bassanio's. The gesture is the scene's emotional climax: a man too moved to face his friend directly. 'Affection wondrous sensible' means an emotion that was powerfully felt and physically visible. The depth of feeling described here exceeds conventional friendship and sits at the heart of the play's exploration of what Antonio and Bassanio mean to each other.

sources.name: Cicero, De Amicitia
sources.citation: Cicero, De Amicitia (On Friendship) 80: the true friend as 'tamquam alter idem,' a second self; the basis for the Renaissance friendship ideal.

sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (Oxford, 1911; rev. Eagleson 1986), s.v. 'sensible' sense 1: 'perceptible to the senses, visible, tangible.'

anchor_text: comes to his election presently
summary: 'Election' here means the act of choosing — Arragon is about to make his selection from the three caskets. 'Presently' means immediately, not 'in a little while' as it does in modern English.

Both glosses are textbook-accurate: 'election' as choosing and 'presently' as immediately are standard Elizabethan usage, confirmed by the scene context ('And comes to his election presently' meaning he arrives at once to make his choice).

anchor_text: I address'd me
summary: 'Address'd me' means he has prepared or composed himself — the reflexive construction 'address oneself' meant to make ready for an action. Arragon says he has braced himself for the choice.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'address' (to make ready, prepare oneself).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1057
Onions s.v. 'address' (to make ready, prepare oneself) is a documented entry that correctly supports the reflexive gloss.
The reflexive 'address'd me' meaning 'prepared/composed myself' is well-attested Shakespearean usage and fits the context exactly — Arragon says he has made ready before invoking Fortune.

anchor_text: fool multitude, that choose by show
summary: Arragon scorns the 'fool multitude' who judge by outward show rather than inner worth, and refuses to 'jump with' (agree with) the common crowd. His disdain for the masses is ironic: his self-congratulatory logic leads him straight to the silver casket and a fool's portrait, proving him the greatest fool of all.
detail: The irony is sharp and structural. Arragon reasons that since 'many men' desire what is in the gold casket, he will not touch it — the crowd is stupid, he is not the crowd. He then selects 'as much as he deserves,' which the scroll mocks by handing him a blinking idiot's portrait. Shakespeare arranges the casket scenes so that each prince's reasoning is simultaneously convincing and self-damning: Morocco chose gold out of worldly pride; Arragon chooses silver out of intellectual pride. Both are forms of vanity, and both fail. Bassanio, who wins, chooses lead precisely by refusing all self-serving logic.

sources.name: Bevington, ed., The Merchant of Venice
sources.citation: Bevington, David, ed. The Merchant of Venice. Bantam, 1988, note to 2.9.25-32 (Arragon's self-defeating rejection of 'the fool multitude').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1064

Bevington's 1988 Bantam Merchant of Venice exists and his note range is plausible, but the specific note to '2.9.25-32' cannot be independently verified and the Bantam edition's scholarly depth for this kind of structural observation is uncertain; the interpretation is defensible but the single secondary-edition source is unverifiable without the physical book.

The ironic structure — Arragon condemns the crowd for shallow choosing then immediately makes his own pride-driven error — is the mainstream reading of this scene, and the comparison of Morocco's pride of wealth with Arragon's pride of intellect as parallel vanities is a sound, widely-accepted dramatic interpretation.

anchor_text: like the martlet, Builds in the weather on the outward wall
summary: The martlet (also spelled 'martinet') is a swift or house-martin, a small bird that nests on the exposed outer walls of buildings rather than in protected eaves. Arragon uses it as a figure for foolish people who build their lives on surfaces exposed to storms and chance — 'in the force and road of casualty' means in the direct path of misfortune.
detail: The martlet has a second life in Elizabethan heraldry: it was the device assigned to fourth sons (who inherit nothing) and was drawn without feet, as though it could never land — a figure for the man without a foothold who must keep flying. Shakespeare's audience would catch both the literal nesting-bird and the heraldic landless wanderer. In either reading the image underscores the precariousness of choosing by outward show. 'Road' in 'road of casualty' carries its older sense of a path or a raid — the full force of chance bearing down on you.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'martlet' n.1 (house-martin, Delichon urbica) and n.2 (heraldic device of a footless bird, assigned to fourth sons in English armory).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'casualty' (accident, mischance; OED sense 1b).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1066
OED s.v. 'martlet' n.1 (house-martin) and n.2 (heraldic footless bird for fourth sons) are real entries confirmed by multiple heraldic reference sources; Onions s.v. 'casualty' is a documented entry.

The literal bird-nesting reading is secure, but the heraldic fourth-son claim requires caution: the heraldic martlet (footless bird assigned to younger sons) was a real device, yet whether a theatre audience would reliably activate both meanings simultaneously, and whether 'fourth sons' specifically (rather than younger sons generally) is the right specification, is contested enough to mark uncertain rather than high-confidence.

anchor_text: estates, degrees, and offices / Were not deriv'd corruptly
summary: Arragon wishes that rank ('estates'), social position ('degrees'), and public posts ('offices') were earned by merit rather than inherited corruptly. 'How many then should cover that stand bare' means: how many low-born people of true worth would then be entitled to keep their hats on (a mark of honour) before those who now receive that deference with none of the worth to deserve it. The complaint was a live one in Elizabethan England, where office and title were bought, inherited, or granted by favour.
detail: The custom of 'covering' (wearing a hat) versus 'standing bare' (removing the hat) was the basic bodily grammar of Elizabethan rank: inferiors uncovered before superiors. Arragon fantasises a world in which that grammar reflects inner worth rather than birth. The speech is dramatically double-edged: Arragon is partly right that 'clear honour' should be 'purchas'd by the merit of the wearer,' but his self-assessment — that he, Arragon, is the man who deserves Portia — is proved laughably wrong the moment he opens the casket.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary

sources.name: OED

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1079
Onions s.v. 'cover' and 'degree' and OED s.v. 'bare' (bareheaded) are real, well-attested entries that correctly support the covering/standing-bare social custom described.

The covering/standing-bare custom as a marker of rank is well-documented Elizabethan social practice, and the reading of Arragon's speech as simultaneously valid social critique and self-damning irony is the mainstream scholarly interpretation.

anchor_text: The fire seven times tried this; / Seven times tried that judgment is
summary: The scroll inside the silver casket opens by invoking the image of silver 'tried' (refined, tested) seven times in fire -- a biblical figure for perfect purity. Psalm 12:6 declares that the words of God are 'as the silver, tried in a furnace of earth, fined seven fold' (Geneva 1599). The casket that looks purest, tried seven times, is still only silver; and the judgment that has never chosen amiss has just chosen wrong.

Psalm 12:6 is the standard biblical source for the 'silver tried seven times in fire' image, the Geneva 1599 wording is quoted correctly, and the ironic application of scriptural purity-language to a failed chooser is a defensible reading supported by the scroll's mock-flattery structure.

anchor_text: There be fools alive, I wis
summary: 'I wis' is an archaic expression meaning 'certainly' or 'indeed.' It derives from the Old English verb 'witan,' to know, and was already old-fashioned in Shakespeare's time — appropriate here since the scroll is written in a mock-antique, rhyming verse form. The line means: 'There are fools alive, to be sure.'

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'iwis' adv. (certainly, assuredly; Old English gewis): archaic in Shakespeare's time, used chiefly in verse.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1107
OED s.v. 'iwis' adv. (certainly, assuredly; from Old English gewis) is a real entry that correctly supports the gloss and the note that it was archaic in Shakespeare's time.

'I wis' as an archaic adverb meaning 'certainly/indeed' from OE 'gewis' is standard lexicography, and its mock-antique register fitting the scroll's rhyming verse is a sound, uncontroversial observation.

anchor_text: the candle sing'd the moth
summary: Portia draws on a proverbial comparison: moths are attracted to candle flames and are burned by the very thing that draws them. The saying compressed the casket plot into a single image — the suitors are moths lured to what they think is light, and they are singed for their presumption. 'Deliberate fools' (TLN 1119) sharpens the irony: the more carefully they reason, the more certainly they fail.

sources.name: Tilley, A Dictionary of the Proverbs
sources.citation: Tilley, M. P. A Dictionary of the Proverbs in England in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries (University of Michigan Press, 1950): the proverb that the fly/moth that plays with the candle singes its wings (the moth-and-candle figure), listed as proverbial.

The moth-and-candle proverb is well-attested in Tilley and the gloss accurately captures its application to Arragon; 'deliberate fools' as an ironic intensifier pointing to the self-defeating nature of careful wrong reasoning is a mainstream reading.

anchor_text: Hanging and wiving goes by destiny
summary: Nerissa quotes a proverbial saying: marriage ('wiving') and hanging — both irreversible fates, both things one cannot escape when destined — are governed by fate, not choice. The dark comic pairing of marriage with execution was a stock Elizabethan joke. Coming just after Arragon departs humiliated, the proverb also reassures Portia: neither she nor Bassanio can force the outcome; destiny will bring the right man.
detail: The saying belongs to a family of proverbs equating marriage with doom — punning on the irreversibility of both the noose and the wedding vow, and on the idea that a bad wife was a kind of hanging anyway. It also recalls the oath every suitor must take before choosing: if he fails, he must never woo another woman in his life (TLN 1051). In that sense the casket lottery itself resembles a kind of fate-machine — the right suitor will come when destiny (and Portia's father's wisdom) wills it.

sources.name: Tilley, A Dictionary of the Proverbs
sources.citation: Tilley, M. P. A Dictionary of the Proverbs in England in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries. University of Michigan Press, 1950. H118: 'Hanging and wiving go by destiny.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1122

The proverb 'Hanging and wiving go by destiny' is well-attested since Heywood (1546) and appears in Tilley's dictionary; H118 is plausible as a Tilley H-entry and the proverb's existence and Elizabethan currency are not in doubt.

The proverb is recorded in Tilley, the dark-comic pairing of marriage and execution is a standard Elizabethan conceit, and the function of the line as reassurance about destiny (in context after Arragon's departure) is a plausible and defensible reading; nothing here overreaches.

anchor_text: sensible regreets; / To wit,--besides commends and courteous breath
summary: 'Sensible regreets' means tangible, physical greetings — gifts you can touch ('sensible' = perceptible to the senses), as opposed to mere words. 'Commends' means commendations, compliments. 'Courteous breath' is polite speech. The servant is reporting that Bassanio's messenger brings both spoken greetings and actual presents.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'sensible' adj. (perceptible to the senses, tangible) and s.v. 'regret' n. (greeting, salutation — archaic in this sense by the 17th century).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1129
Onions s.v. 'sensible' (perceptible to the senses) and s.v. 'regret' (greeting, salutation — archaic) are real entries that correctly support both glosses.
'Sensible' as tangible/perceptible-to-the-senses and 'regreets' as greetings/salutations are straightforward archaic-vocabulary glosses that fit the text exactly and are confirmed by Onions.

anchor_text: this fore-spurrer comes before his lord
summary: A 'fore-spurrer' is a forerunner who rides ahead — literally one who spurs his horse forward in advance of the main party to announce or prepare for its arrival. The servant is calling Bassanio's young messenger a herald or advance man who signals his lord's imminent approach.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'forspurrer' n. (one who rides ahead; a forerunner); rare, with this passage as a primary citation.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1135
OED s.v. 'forspurrer' (one who rides ahead; a forerunner) is a real, rare entry for which this Merchant of Venice passage is among the primary citations, correctly supporting the gloss.
'Fore-spurrer' as a forerunner who rides ahead fits the scene context (the servant arriving before Bassanio's party) and the OED cites this passage; the gloss is accurate and modest.

anchor_text: Thou spend'st such high-day wit in praising him
summary: 'High-day' means festive or holiday, the best and most elaborate. Portia is teasing the servant for burning his most extravagant, show-off eloquence ('high-day wit') on praise of Bassanio's messenger — as if he is saving his fine Sunday speech for this one young man. The implication is that his enthusiasm betrays a personal partiality for whoever this visitor is.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'high-day' adj. (belonging to a holiday or festival; hence extravagant, showy): used of language or dress that is best-occasion quality.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1138
OED s.v. 'high-day' adj. (belonging to a holiday or festival; extravagant, showy) is a real entry that correctly supports the gloss of festive or best-occasion quality.

'High-day' as holiday/festive-best is well-attested, and Portia's teasing that the servant is spending his finest eloquence on the young visitor is directly supported by the surrounding dialogue ('Thou wilt say anon he is some kin to thee').

anchor_text: Quick Cupid's post that comes so mannerly
summary: A 'post' was a mounted courier who rode quickly ('quick') between posts along a road — the fastest messenger of the period. Portia calls Bassanio's young envoy 'Cupid's post,' meaning Love's own swift messenger. Cupid was the Roman god of love, here imagined as the master who has sent this handsome young man ahead to announce Bassanio. Nerissa's closing line ('Bassanio, lord Love, if thy will it be!') confirms that she and Portia both believe and hope this suitor is the right one.
detail: Cupid as a winged, swift messenger of love was a standard emblem in Renaissance poetry and painting. The phrase fuses two common images: the post-rider (the fastest human messenger, associated with urgent news and young men on horseback) and the Cupid-figure who carries the arrow or letter of love between hearts. Portia's restraint — 'No more, I pray thee' — and her exclamation that she is 'half afeard' the servant loves this visitor himself, before breaking into eager anticipation, is among her most open moments of feeling in the play.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.468-474 (Cupid with his golden and leaden arrows — the standard classical image of Cupid as the swift agent of love, familiar in Renaissance emblem books and poetry).

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'post' n.3 (a courier riding in relays, the fastest mail-carrier; hence any swift messenger).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1140

The Ovid Metamorphoses golden/leaden arrows passage is real and falls in the 1.452-567 range, but the cited line numbers 1.468-474 appear slightly off (the arrows description is closer to 1.466-471 in Latin editions); OED s.v. 'post' n.3 is a genuine entry — the Ovid citation is not fabricated but the line numbers are imprecise enough to flag.

Calling Bassanio's messenger 'Cupid's post' (Love's swift courier) is a straightforward Renaissance emblem conceit; the Ovid citation for Cupid's arrows is a loose but acceptable reference to the standard classical Cupid image, and Nerissa's closing line confirms the romantic anticipation the annotation describes.

anchor_text: wrack'd on the narrow seas; the Goodwins
summary: The Goodwin Sands is a large sandbank off the Kent coast in the Strait of Dover (the 'narrow seas'), notorious for wrecking ships. The word 'wrack'd' means 'wrecked.' Salarino is reporting a rumor that Antonio has lost a ship on one of England's most feared hazards.
detail: The Goodwin Sands lie roughly five miles off Deal in Kent and have claimed hundreds of vessels over the centuries. The name was current in Elizabethan navigation and would have needed no explanation for Shakespeare's London audience. The phrase 'narrow seas' was the standard English term for the English Channel and the Strait of Dover. The detail anchors the play's Atlantic-Mediterranean trade world in a danger that the audience knew at first hand.

sources.name: Sugden, Topographical Dictionary to Shakespeare
sources.citation: Edward H. Sugden, A Topographical Dictionary to the Works of Shakespeare and His Fellow Dramatists (1925), s.v. 'Goodwin Sands.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1144

Sugden's Topographical Dictionary (1925) is a real and standard Shakespearean topographical reference; the Goodwin Sands are confirmed approximately 5-6 miles off Deal in Kent, and 'narrow seas' for the Strait of Dover is well-attested Elizabethan usage.
The Goodwin Sands identification, 'narrow seas' as the Strait of Dover/Channel, and 'wrack'd' as 'wrecked' are all standard and well-attested; nothing here overreaches.

anchor_text: gossip Report be an honest woman
summary: Salarino personifies Rumour as 'gossip Report' — a garrulous neighborhood woman who spreads news. A 'gossip' was originally a godparent or close female friend, but by Shakespeare's day it had come to mean a woman who talks freely about other people's affairs. The joke is that Salarino hopes she is lying, which would mean Antonio's ship is safe.
detail: Personifying Rumour as a woman with a reputation for truthfulness or dishonesty is a classical and Renaissance convention: Virgil's Fama (Aeneid 4.173-188) and Ovid's House of Rumour (Metamorphoses 12.39-63) are the ancient types. In English drama the figure appears as the painted Induction-speaker of Henry IV Part 2. Here the register is comic and domestic: Salarino shrinks Virgil's monstrous deity to a neighborhood gossip who knaps (bites) ginger and weeps crocodile tears over dead husbands.

sources.name: OED s.v. gossip
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'gossip,' sense 2a: a woman who talks much about others, and sense 1: a godparent or close friend (the original meaning).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1147

The OED etymology of 'gossip' (from godparent/close female friend to idle talker) is accurate and the cited senses 1 and 2a are real; the Virgil Aeneid 4.173-188 and Ovid Metamorphoses 12.39-63 references in the detail text are both confirmed accurate, though they appear only as contextual enrichment and are not cited in the sources array.

Personifying Rumour as a garrulous woman is sound, and the etymology from godparent to chatterbox is accurate OED sense; the Virgil/Ovid parallels are noted appropriately as background rather than sources.

anchor_text: the devil cross my prayer, for here he comes in the likeness of a Jew
summary: Salanio's joke that saying 'amen' will attract the devil — who has conveniently arrived 'in the likeness of a Jew' — relies on a specific Elizabethan slur: Jews were routinely equated with the devil in Christian folk-demonology. The line is a blunt expression of the antisemitism the play both reproduces and, in Shylock's later speeches, calls into question.
detail: The identification of Jews with the devil was widespread in medieval and early modern Christian culture, drawing on passages such as John 8:44 ('Ye are of your father the devil') and on the iconography of the so-called 'Judensau' and the mystery plays where Jewish figures wore devil-red or demonic masks. Because Jews had been expelled from England since 1290, the 'Jew' most Elizabethans knew was a stage caricature shaped by these traditions. Shakespeare builds Salanio's casual cruelty into the texture of Venetian daily life to establish the humiliation Shylock then anatomizes in the 'Hath not a Jew eyes' speech.

sources.name: Shapiro, Shakespeare and the Jews
sources.citation: James Shapiro, Shakespeare and the Jews (1996), ch. 2-3 (the devil-Jew identification in English popular culture).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1159

Shapiro's Shakespeare and the Jews (1996) is real and chapters 2-3 ('Myths, Histories, Consequences' and 'The Jewish Crime') do cover the cultural construction of Jews in English popular imagination including the devil-Jew identification; John 8:44 is accurately cited.

The devil-Jew conflation in Elizabethan folk-demonology is well-documented, and the reading that the play both reproduces and ironizes it through the 'Hath not a Jew eyes' speech is mainstream in the critical tradition; no overreach.

anchor_text: To bait fish withal: if it will feed nothing else, it will feed my revenge
summary: 'Bait' here means to use as bait — to put on a hook to attract fish. 'Withal' is an archaic form meaning 'with it.' Shylock is answering the sneering question 'what's that [a pound of flesh] good for?' with savage sarcasm: if Antonio's flesh is too worthless to serve any other purpose, at least it will satisfy his revenge.
detail: The cold precision of 'To bait fish withal' — the most utilitarian possible use for a human body — signals Shylock's fury operating through a rigidly controlled syntax. The line pivots immediately from the grotesque (fish-bait) to the psychological ('feed my revenge'), drawing a parallel between the two kinds of appetite. The same hard monosyllabic logic powers the 'Hath not a Jew eyes' speech that follows.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. bait
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874), s.v. 'bait,' sense 1: to furnish or cover with bait.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1184

Alexander Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874) is a real and standard reference; 'bait' as a verb meaning to furnish with bait (fishing sense) is a genuine lexicographic sense well-supported by this work.
'Bait withal' as 'use as bait' and 'withal' as 'with it' are correct; the interpretive gloss (savage sarcasm pivoting from grotesque to psychological) accurately follows the text's movement.

anchor_text: Hath not a Jew eyes? Hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses
summary: Shylock builds his case for shared humanity through a series of rapid questions, each beginning 'Hath not' or 'If.' This rhetorical figure — repeating the same word or phrase at the start of successive clauses — is called anaphora. The repeated 'Hath not a Jew' both hammers its point and performs Shylock's exhaustion at having to prove the obvious.
detail: The speech runs from TLN 1188 to 1200 and is among the most discussed passages in Shakespeare. The anaphora ('Hath not a Jew eyes... hands... organs... dimensions... senses... affections... passions') is augmented by isocolon — parallel clauses of equal length ('fed with the same food, hurt with the same weapons, subject to the same diseases'). This balance is then broken when the speech turns from shared suffering to shared capacity for revenge: 'And if you wrong us, shall we not revenge?' The formal equality implied by the rhetoric dissolves into the play's darkest irony — shared humanity becomes a shared logic of retaliation. The passage gives the despised figure a protest that no earlier Elizabethan stage-Jew possessed, yet it ends by grounding revenge in the principle of imitation: 'The villainy you teach me I will execute.' See the reference card on the 'Jew' on the Elizabethan stage.

sources.name: Lanham, A Handlist of Rhetorical Terms
sources.citation: Richard A. Lanham, A Handlist of Rhetorical Terms, 2nd ed. (1991), s.v. 'anaphora' and 'isocolon.'

sources.name: Shapiro, Shakespeare and the Jews
sources.citation: James Shapiro, Shakespeare and the Jews (1996), ch. 4 (the 'Hath not a Jew eyes' speech in its theatrical and cultural context).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1188

Lanham's Handlist of Rhetorical Terms (2nd ed., 1991) is confirmed real and covers both anaphora and isocolon; Shapiro ch. 4 'The Pound of Flesh' is confirmed and directly addresses this speech in its theatrical and cultural context.

Identifying anaphora and isocolon is accurate to the speech's structure, and the observation that the balanced rhetoric collapses into a logic of revenge is a well-established and textually defensible reading.

anchor_text: The curse never fell upon our nation till now
summary: Shylock interprets Jessica's theft and flight as a biblical 'curse' upon the Jewish people. The idea that Jews are under a curse was a pervasive Christian reading of Deuteronomy 28 and Matthew 27:25 ('His blood be on us, and on our children'). Here Shylock voices this framework from the inside — his personal disaster becomes a communal divine punishment.
detail: Deuteronomy 28:15-68 (Geneva 1599) lists catastrophes that will befall Israel if it breaks covenant with God, including the loss of children and property. Matthew 27:25 was the verse Christian theology used to claim that Jews collectively accepted guilt for the Crucifixion, and the 'curse' was invoked to explain every Jewish suffering as divinely ordained punishment. That Shylock uses this framework to describe his own grief is deeply ambivalent: he has so thoroughly internalized the dominant culture's reading of Jewish history that his daughter's elopement looks to him like theological warrant. The line precedes his anguished wish that Jessica were 'dead at my foot' with the jewels — an outburst that auditors have always found as much grief as greed.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Deuteronomy 28:15 (Geneva 1599): 'But if thou wilt not obey the voice of the Lord thy God... all these curses shall come upon thee.' Matthew 27:25 (Geneva 1599): 'Then answered all the people, and said, His blood be on us, and on our children.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1210

Both Geneva Bible citations check out: Deuteronomy 28:15 Geneva 1599 reads 'But if thou wilt not obey the voice of the Lord thy God... all these curses shall come upon thee,' and Matthew 27:25 reads 'His blood be on us, and on our children' — both accurately quoted and directly supportive of the annotation's claims.

Attributing Shylock's phrase to his internalization of the Deuteronomy 28 / Matthew 27:25 Christian curse-narrative is a plausible scholarly reading, but the text is equally consistent with a more generic Hebrew concept of communal misfortune; presenting it as Shylock voicing the Christian theological framework 'from the inside' is a significant interpretive step that is contested and should not be marked 'medium' confidence implying near-certainty.

anchor_text: turquoise; I had it of Leah when I was a bachelor
summary: Leah is Shylock's dead wife — the only time she is named in the play. The turquoise was the only item among his losses to which Shylock assigns sentimental value rather than a price. Elizabethan gem-lore held that turquoise changed color with the wearer's health and could secure the love of a spouse — making it an apt keepsake from a wife who is gone.
detail: The turquoise (or 'turkeystone' in contemporary spelling) was among the most prized stones in Elizabethan jewelry, imported through Turkey from Persia. Popular lapidaries such as Thomas Nicols's A Lapidary (1652, drawing on earlier sources) credited it with the ability to protect against the evil eye, strengthen the wearer, and indicate the state of a beloved's health by changing color. For Shylock this stone is not a monetary asset — uniquely in this scene he explicitly refuses a monetary valuation ('I would not have given it for a wilderness of monkeys') — which makes the loss to Jessica's casual trade for a monkey the sharpest of the scene's many reversals.

sources.name: Nicols, A Lapidary (1652)
sources.citation: Thomas Nicols, A Lapidary: or, The History of Pretious Stones (1652), ch. on 'Turkois' (drawing on earlier Renaissance lapidaries including Marbodus and Anselmus Boetius).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1239

Thomas Nicols' A Lapidary (1652) is a real work and does discuss turquoise color-change properties, and the referenced earlier authors Marbodius and Anselmus Boëtius de Boodt are real lapidary writers; however, the specific claim that the turquoise was believed to 'secure the love of a spouse' cannot be confirmed from available sources, and Nicols (1652) postdates the play by about 54 years, making him a secondary witness to Elizabethan gem-lore at best.

Leah as Shylock's dead wife, the turquoise as a sentimental keepsake, and its lapidary associations (health-indicator, love-token) are all defensible; the contrast with the monkey trade is clearly supported by the text.

anchor_text: fee me an officer; bespeak him a fortnight before
summary: 'Fee me an officer' means 'hire (retain with a fee) an officer of the law — a bailiff or sergeant — for me.' 'Bespeak him a fortnight before' means 'engage him two weeks in advance.' Shylock is planning ahead to have a legal constable ready to arrest Antonio the moment the bond falls due.
detail: An 'officer' in this legal context is a serjeant or catchpole — a court officer authorized to make arrests for debt. To 'fee' him is to pay a retaining fee, binding him to act on a given day. Shylock's cold precision in thinking two weeks ahead is characteristic: his grief for Jessica and the ring immediately gives way to the practical mechanics of revenge. The detail establishes that this is not an impulsive threat but a calculated legal maneuver.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. fee
sources.citation: Alexander Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874), s.v. 'fee,' verb sense: to bribe or retain by paying a fee.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. bespeak
sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. R. D. Eagleson (1986), s.v. 'bespeak': to engage in advance.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1242

Both Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874) for 'fee' (to retain by paying a fee) and Onions' Shakespeare Glossary (rev. Eagleson, 1986) for 'bespeak' (to engage in advance, confirmed via Perseus Digital Library) are real standard references that support the cited senses.
'Fee' as retain by payment and 'bespeak a fortnight before' as engage in advance are accurately glossed; the characterization of cold premeditation is well-grounded in the text.

anchor_text: I pray you tarry; pause a day or two
summary: Portia asks Bassanio to delay the casket choice. 'Tarry' means to wait or stay. She is bound by her father's will not to hint at the right casket, yet she wants to keep him near — her opening speeches balance the constraint against her feeling for him.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'tarry': to delay, wait, or remain.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1247
Onions s.v. 'tarry' is a standard, real lexicographical entry that supports the gloss given.
Accurate gloss: 'tarry' does mean to wait/stay, and the surrounding lines plainly show Portia delaying Bassanio while constrained by her oath — the interpretation follows directly from the text.

anchor_text: a maiden hath no tongue but thought
summary: Portia invokes the Elizabethan ideal that a well-bred unmarried woman expresses herself only in private thought, not in open speech. The phrase half-excuses her oblique way of talking: convention forbids her from speaking directly what she feels.
detail: The idea that a modest woman's feelings belong to 'thought' — silent inner life — rather than public utterance belongs to the broader Elizabethan conduct-book ideal of female chastity extended to speech. Portia is being ironic about her own constraint: she is in fact speaking at some length, but must avoid the directness that would violate both the convention and her oath to honour her father's will.

sources.name: Vives, Instruction of a Christian Woman
sources.citation: Juan Luis Vives, Instruction of a Christian Woman (1524; trans. Richard Hyrde, 1529), on female modesty and the restraint of speech as a virtue paired with chastity.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1254
Vives, Instruction of a Christian Woman (Latin 1524, trans. Hyrde 1529) is a real and widely-cited Elizabethan conduct-book source for the ideal of feminine verbal restraint paired with chastity.

Sound reading: Portia explicitly apologizes for speaking at length despite convention forbidding a modest maid's direct expression — the conduct-book context is appropriate and the irony noted is textually grounded.

anchor_text: I am forsworn; So will I never be
summary: To be 'forsworn' is to have broken a solemn oath. Portia says she could teach Bassanio how to choose right — but that would mean breaking the oath she swore to honour her father's will, and she refuses to do that.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'forsworn': having sworn falsely, having violated one's oath.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1257
Onions s.v. 'forsworn' is a real entry supporting the definition given.
'Forsworn' plainly means oath-broken in this context, and the text confirms Portia declines to hint at the right casket specifically to avoid breaking her sworn commitment to her father's will.

anchor_text: Beshrew your eyes, They have o'erlook'd me
summary: 'Beshrew' is a mild curse, roughly 'a plague on' or 'shame on.' 'O'erlook'd' means bewitched — the belief that certain gazes, especially from someone in love, could cast a spell on the person looked at. Portia says Bassanio's eyes have enchanted her so she is divided against herself.
detail: The belief in the evil or amorous eye (Latin fascinatio) was widely current in the Renaissance; to be 'overlooked' was to be charmed or bewitched by another's gaze. Portia's 'divided me' (the next line) develops the conceit: the bewitchment has split her in two — one half that is his, one half she claims as her own but which is really his too. The phrasing anticipates her formal self-surrender speech later in the scene.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'overlook': to bewitch by the evil eye; and s.v. 'beshrew': mild imprecation, 'a plague on.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1260
Onions carries both s.v. 'overlook' (bewitch by the evil eye) and s.v. 'beshrew' (mild imprecation), correctly glossed here.

'O'erlook'd' as bewitched by the gaze is well-attested in Elizabethan usage and fits the line; the detail about the fascinatio belief and Portia's 'divided me' follow-through are textually supportable.

anchor_text: 'tis to peise the time, To eke it
summary: 'Peise' (or poise) means to weigh down or retard; 'eke' means to stretch out or extend. Portia admits she has been talking only to slow time and keep Bassanio from the caskets a little longer.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874), s.v. 'peise': to weigh down, to delay by adding weight; and s.v. 'eke': to stretch out, to prolong.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1268
Schmidt s.v. 'peise' and s.v. 'eke' are real entries; the glosses match standard lexicographical usage.
Both glosses are correct: 'peise' as weigh down/retard and 'eke' as stretch out are standard archaic meanings that the context ('I speak too long, but 'tis to peise the time') fully corroborates.

anchor_text: I live upon the rack
summary: The rack was a torture device that stretched a prisoner's body to force a confession. Bassanio says the waiting is torture; Portia picks up the image by asking what 'treason' is mixed in with his love — on the rack, prisoners were forced to confess to crimes. The exchange turns courtship briefly into an interrogation scene.
detail: The rack (stretching rack) was a legal instrument of the English state under special warrant from the Privy Council; it was used to extract confessions in cases of treason. The lovers' wordplay runs the metaphor through: Portia asks for his 'confession,' Bassanio says 'Promise me life' (the rack-victim begging mercy before confessing), and she says 'confess and live' — mimicking the magistrate's promise of clemency for a cooperative prisoner. The wit is that their 'treason' turns out to be love itself.

sources.name: Jardine, Reading Shakespeare Historically
sources.citation: Jardine, Lisa, Reading Shakespeare Historically (Routledge, 1996), on torture and interrogation in Elizabethan legal culture.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1272

Jardine, Reading Shakespeare Historically (Routledge, 1996) is a real book that addresses Elizabethan legal culture including torture; the claim about the rack and treason confessions is historically sound.
The rack-as-torture extended metaphor is explicitly developed in the text across TLN 1272–1286 (confess, treason, promise me life, confess and live), making this a close reading, not an over-reading.

anchor_text: young Alcides when he did redeem The virgin tribute paid by howling Troy
summary: 'Alcides' is Hercules, named for his grandfather Alcaeus. Portia compares Bassanio choosing her casket to Hercules rescuing Hesione: the city of Troy was forced to offer a young woman as tribute to a sea-monster, and Hercules killed the monster and freed her. Portia is the 'sacrifice,' Bassanio is the hero, and Nerissa and the attendants are the 'Dardanian wives' watching from the shore.

anchor_text: Tell me where is fancy bred, Or in the heart or in the head
summary: 'Fancy' means infatuation or superficial love -- love driven by what the eye sees, not the heart knows. The song argues that fancy is 'engend'red in the eyes' and dies in 'the cradle where it lies,' warning against love of outward show. Three of its rhymes -- bred, head, nourished, fed, lies -- end on sounds close to 'lead.' Some editors argue the song tips Bassanio toward the lead casket; others read it as Portia's household music with no intended hint.
detail: The word 'fancy' in Elizabethan usage could mean both love in general and specifically a passing, superficial infatuation rooted in the senses rather than judgment. The song's argument -- that sight-driven love is born and dies quickly -- aligns perfectly with Bassanio's casket speech, which rejects 'ornament' and 'outward show.' Whether the rhymes (bred/head/nourished all potentially rhyming with 'lead') are an intended cheat by Portia, a pointed coincidence, or nothing at all has been debated since the eighteenth century. The three-caskets source in the Gesta Romanorum makes no provision for such a hint.

sources.citation: Bullough, Geoffrey, Narrative and Dramatic Sources of Shakespeare, vol. 1 (Routledge, 1957), on the Gesta Romanorum casket tale and the question of the song's rhymes.

anchor_text: The world is still deceiv'd with ornament
summary: Bassanio delivers a formal speech on the gap between appearance and reality — one of the play's central themes. He works through examples: corrupt legal arguments dressed in a fine voice, wrong religious doctrine blessed by a pious face, cowardice hidden beneath a soldier's beard. Each case shows the same pattern: bad content disguised by attractive form. The speech is an extended version of the proverb 'All that glisters is not gold' (what Morocco found on the gold casket).

sources.name: Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice (text)
sources.citation: The Merchant of Venice 3.2.73-101 (Bassanio's casket speech): the accumulated examples -- law, religion, beauty, cowardice -- of 'ornament' as 'the seeming truth which cunning times put on / To entrap the wisest,' culminating in his rejection of gold and silver.

The identification of the rhetorical device as accumulation of parallel examples and the reading of it as implicit criticism of Morocco and Arragon are mainstream and textually grounded; nothing here overreaches.

anchor_text: The beards of Hercules and frowning Mars; Who, inward search'd, have livers white as milk
summary: Hercules and Mars (Ares in Greek) were the classical emblems of strength and war. Bassanio says that cowards grow full beards to look like these heroes, but when examined inside ('inward search'd'), their livers are 'white as milk.' The liver was thought to be the seat of courage; a pale, bloodless liver meant cowardice.
detail: In humoral physiology the liver produced blood and courage; a deficient liver meant the person lacked spirit. 'White-livered' remained a proverbial insult for centuries. Wearing long beards to imitate legendary warriors was a recognized form of social performance; Bassanio's point is that the costume of courage (the beard, the look) is itself an 'ornament' that conceals the inner reality. Hercules wears his club and lion-skin; Mars his armour and scowl — but these are the casket-speech's theme of misleading show applied to human biology.

sources.name: Bright, A Treatise of Melancholie (1586)
sources.citation: Timothy Bright, A Treatise of Melancholie (London, 1586), on the humoral physiology of the liver as the seat of courage and the significance of a pale liver.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1333

The white-liver as cowardice in humoral physiology is well-established, and the application to 'beards of Hercules and frowning Mars' as false warrior-ornament fits the casket speech's running theme exactly.

anchor_text: these assume but valour's excrement
summary: 'Excrement' here means outgrowth — what grows outward from the body, such as hair, nails, or a beard. Cowards 'assume' (put on) the outward growth of bravery — i.e., a warrior's beard — to seem formidable. The modern meaning of the word did not dominate in Shakespeare's day.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'excrement': outgrowth from the body, such as hair or beard (from Latin excrementum, outgrowth).

'Excrement' as bodily outgrowth (hair, nails, beard) is the dominant Elizabethan sense in this context and Onions confirms it; the clarification that the modern meaning did not dominate is accurate and useful.

anchor_text: 'tis purchas'd by the weight: Which therein works a miracle in nature, Making them lightest that wear most of it
summary: Bassanio says cosmetics are sold 'by the weight' — literally, the heaviest jars cost most. The pun is that women who use the most cosmetic are therefore the 'lightest' — a bawdy double meaning in which 'light' means both physically light (not heavy) and sexually loose. The wordplay continues the casket speech's attack on purchased beauty.
detail: The bawdy sense of 'light' for a sexually available woman was common currency in Elizabethan English (cf. Romeo and Juliet 2.4: 'a light wench... lightens our darkness'). The pun does triple work: the literal physics (weight purchased makes them light), the moral charge (cosmetics = vanity = looseness), and the relevance to the casket test (the gold and silver caskets are literally heavier but contain less worth than the dull lead). Editors from the eighteenth century onward have noted the bawdy undercurrent here.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1874), s.v. 'light': wanton, unchaste — a standard Elizabethan pun.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1337

The 'lightest' pun on sexually loose is a genuine and well-documented Elizabethan double meaning (cf. R&J), and the text's 'purchased by the weight' / 'making them lightest that wear most' invites exactly this wordplay.

anchor_text: those crisped snaky golden locks Which make such wanton gambols with the wind, Upon supposed fairness
summary: Bassanio argues that elaborately curled golden hair is often borrowed — cut from a dead woman's head and fashioned into a wig or hair-piece. 'Supposed fairness' means assumed or false beauty. The practice of selling dead women's hair to wigmakers was documented in Elizabethan London. Bassanio presents it as another form of the 'ornament' theme: the skull that grew those locks is now in the grave.
detail: 'Crisped' means artificially curled or frizzed. The hair-trade in Elizabethan England included human hair from the living and recently dead; hairpieces were worn by both men and women of fashion. The image that the curls' true owner is 'in the sepulchre' gives the ornament speech its most visceral turn: the most admired feature of a beautiful woman may be a dead person's scalp. The same macabre irony reverses on the gold casket, which contains a death's head.

The reading of 'supposed fairness' as assumed/false beauty and the identification of the hair-trade as the referent (the skull in the sepulchre) are textually explicit ('the dowry of a second head, / The skull that bred them'); the cultural context is defensible.

anchor_text: ornament is but the guiled shore To a most dangerous sea
summary: 'Guiled' means treacherous — a shoreline that looks safe but hides rocks or shoals underneath. In a city of merchants and sailors, the metaphor of a deceptive harbor was resonant. Bassanio stacks this on top of 'an Indian beauty' — a dark complexion veiled by a 'beauteous scarf' of cosmetics, continuing his theme that fine appearance hides danger.

anchor_text: Hard food for Midas, I will none of thee
summary: King Midas of Phrygia was granted the wish that everything he touched would turn to gold — then found he could not eat because his food turned to gold the moment it reached his mouth. Bassanio rejects the gold casket with this allusion: gold is 'hard food,' because it cannot nourish. Ovid tells the story in Metamorphoses.
detail: Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.100-145 tells how Dionysus granted Midas the golden touch as a reward for returning the satyr Silenus; Midas starved until the god told him to wash in the river Pactolus, whose sands turned golden. The phrase 'I will none of thee' is an idiom meaning 'I want nothing to do with you.' By invoking Midas, Bassanio frames gold as a curse — wealth that cannot feed, a metaphor for the useless glittering casket whose prize is a skull. The image resonates with Antonio's merchant-world where the pursuit of gold has created Shylock's bond.

sources.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
sources.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.100-145 (Midas and the golden touch); Arthur Golding's English translation, 1567.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1350

The Midas myth is correctly glossed (golden touch → starvation), the Ovidian reference is appropriate, and 'I will none of thee' as idiom for rejection is accurate; the connection to Shylock's gold-world is a mainstream thematic reading.

anchor_text: thou pale and common drudge 'Tween man and man
summary: Bassanio rejects the silver casket by calling silver the 'pale drudge' that passes between people as coin — the everyday medium of trade and debt. Silver is 'common' because it belongs to everyone, buying and selling all day, unlike gold which is rarer, or lead which is humbler. The image links the silver casket directly to the money-economy — Shylock's world of lending and bonds.

Silver as the everyday coin of commercial exchange is the plain sense of 'pale and common drudge 'tween man and man,' and the link to the money-economy is a textually grounded thematic observation.

anchor_text: green-ey'd jealousy
summary: This is one of Shakespeare's own coinage for jealousy as green-eyed — the color was associated with sickness, envy, and treachery. The later 'green-eyed monster' (Othello 3.3) develops the same image. Here Portia prays that her joy not curdle into jealousy, listing the emotions she wants to shed now that the choice is made.
detail: 'Green' in Elizabethan usage carried associations with unripeness, sickness, and envy; bile (one of the four humours) was associated with yellow-green and with jealousy. The pairing of jealousy with 'green-eyed' passed into common use partly through Shakespeare's own plays.

sources.name: OED s.v. 'green-eyed'
sources.citation: OED, s.v. 'green-eyed,' citing Merchant of Venice 3.2 and Othello 3.3 as early uses; cf. the general Elizabethan association of green with envy and sickness.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1358

The 'green-eyed jealousy' reading is sound, but claiming this is 'one of Shakespeare's own coinages' is an overstatement — the green/envy association predates Shakespeare and the exact phrase may derive from earlier writing; the OED's listing of this play as an early cite does not mean it is the first use or a coinage.

anchor_text: Fair Portia's counterfeit! What demi-god Hath come so near creation
summary: 'Counterfeit' here means painted likeness or portrait — not a fake, but a copy made by art. Bassanio praises the portrait as so lifelike that the painter must be a 'demi-god': only something close to divine could create eyes that seem to move. The word carried no dishonest sense in this context; it was a standard term for a painted likeness.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'counterfeit' (sb.): a portrait, a painted likeness — without pejorative force in this usage.

anchor_text: the painter plays the spider, and hath woven A golden mesh t' entrap the hearts of men
summary: Bassanio compares the painter to a spider whose painted web of Portia's golden hair traps men's hearts faster than real spiders trap gnats. The conceit is that the portrait's beauty is itself a kind of snare — a picture that holds the viewer captive. It glances ironically back at the casket speech's attack on gilded ornament, since even Bassanio is caught by a beautiful image.

anchor_text: The continent and summary of my fortune
summary: 'Continent' here means that which contains or holds something — a vessel or container. Bassanio calls the scroll the container and summing-up of his fate. The word's common geographical meaning (a large landmass) is a secondary sense derived from the same Latin root.

anchor_text: an unlesson'd girl, unschool'd, unpractis'd
summary: Portia formally surrenders herself and all her property to Bassanio, describing herself as an 'unlesson'd,' unschooled girl who submits to him as 'lord, governor, king.' This is the legal language of Elizabethan marriage, in which a woman's property and legal person passed to her husband at the wedding. Portia's self-description as ignorant is deeply ironic — she is the play's most brilliant legal mind.

anchor_text: I give them with this ring, Which when you part from, lose, or give away, Let it presage the ruin of your love
summary: Portia gives Bassanio a ring as a pledge of the marriage, warning that parting with it will mean the ruin of their love. A ring given as a marriage token was a legally and emotionally charged object in Elizabethan practice; losing it was a serious breach. This ring becomes the hinge of the play's Act 5 comic crisis, when Bassanio gives it away to the disguised Portia in the trial scene.
detail: The exchange of rings was central to the Elizabethan betrothal and marriage ceremony; a ring given as a pledge was close to contractually binding. Portia's warning — lose the ring, lose my love — is therefore both affectionate and practical, a bond within a bond. The dramatic irony is set up here: the 'lawyer' who will demand the ring in Act 4 is Portia herself, engineering a test of Bassanio's loyalty.

sources.citation: Dolan, Frances E., ed., The Taming of the Shrew: Texts and Contexts (Bedford, 1996), on betrothal rings and their legal standing in Elizabethan marriage custom. Cf. Swinburne, A Treatise of Spousals (written c. 1600, published 1686).

anchor_text: when your honours mean to solemnize The bargain of your faith
summary: 'Solemnize' means to make formal and official with a ceremony — here, to get married. 'The bargain of your faith' means the contract of your troth-plighting or betrothal. The word 'bargain' reflects the period's habit of framing marriage as a legally binding agreement; 'faith' here means troth, the pledged word.
